title: The Flower
tagline: The four whorls of a bisexual flower, the parts inside each one, and how flowers are arranged on a stalk.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every floral part, inflorescence type and placentation type below is standard botany. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: The flower is the reproductive organ of a flowering plant, and its value to a student lies in learning it as four concentric whorls attached to a swollen base called the receptacle. This chapter builds the flower from the outside in — calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium — naming every part and stating its function, then separates the terms that are constantly tested against one another: bisexual against unisexual, complete against incomplete, actinomorphic against zygomorphic. The second half covers how flowers are arranged on a plant through the major inflorescence types, and where the ovules sit inside the ovary through the five kinds of placentation.

facts.label: Four whorls
facts.value: Calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium, from outside inwards

facts.label: Male part
facts.value: Stamen = filament + anther; anther has two pollen sacs

facts.label: Female part
facts.value: Carpel = stigma + style + ovary; ovary contains ovules

facts.label: Function of the flower
facts.value: To produce pollen and ovules, and so to bring about fertilisation and seed formation

learningOutcomes: Draw and label a bisexual flower with all four whorls and state the function of each part.
Distinguish bisexual from unisexual flowers and complete from incomplete flowers.
Describe the main inflorescence types and how the arrangement affects where pollinating insects land.
Explain the five types of placentation and relate each to the way ovules are attached in the ovary.

learn.title: The four whorls of a bisexual flower

blocks.text: A typical flower is a short shoot bearing four whorls of leaves on a swollen end called the receptacle. The outermost whorl is the calyx, made of green leaf-like sepals that enclose and protect the bud before it opens and, in some flowers, remain to support the fruit. Inside the calyx is the corolla, the whorl of petals, which is often brightly coloured or scented to attract pollinating insects; the sepals together form the calyx and the petals together form the corolla. The third whorl is the androecium, the male part, consisting of stamens, each with a slender filament supporting a two-lobed anther in which pollen grains are produced. The innermost whorl is the gynoecium or pistil, the female part, consisting of carpels; a carpel has a sticky stigma that receives pollen, a slender style, and a swollen ovary at the base containing one or more ovules. A flower in which both androecium and gynoecium are present is bisexual, as in mustard, and it is the model from which all the others are variations.

items.meaning: The swollen base of the flower to which all four whorls are attached.
The outer whorl of sepals; it protects the flower in the bud stage.
The whorl of petals, which attracts insects for pollination.
The male whorl of the flower, made up of stamens.
The female whorl, made up of one or more carpels; also called the pistil.
The structure within the ovary that develops into a seed after fertilisation.

blocks.caption: The four floral whorls
rows: Green, leaf-like, often fused into a cup
Protects the flower in bud; supports the open flower
Filament topped by a two-lobed anther
Anther makes pollen by meiosis; filament holds it up for transfer
Stigma, style and ovary containing ovules
Stigma catches pollen; ovary houses ovules that become seeds

Receptacle and the stalk below it
Supports the flower; the axis through the whorls is the floral axis

items: A bisexual or hermaphrodite flower has both stamens and carpels, as in mustard, pea and hibiscus.
A unisexual flower has only one of the two, so a staminate flower is male and a pistillate flower is female.
A flower lacking one or more whorls is incomplete; the pea flower, which has no calyx, is a standard example.
The anther has two lobes, each with two pollen sacs where pollen grains are formed by meiosis.
The ovary matures into the fruit and each fertilised ovule matures into a seed.
The style is the pathway down which the pollen tube grows from the stigma to the ovule.
Nectar is produced by glands called nectaries, usually at the base of the corolla, and it is the reward that brings insects to the flower.
Flowers that are scented and brightly coloured are adapted for insect pollination, while wind-pollinated flowers are small, pale and produce abundant lightweight pollen.

items.text: Mustard has a complete, bisexual flower with four sepals, four petals, six stamens and a superior ovary made of two fused carpels.
items.note: Counting whorls in a familiar flower makes the general plan concrete.

items.text: A coconut palm has separate male and female flowers on the same plant, so it is monoecious; the papaya bears male flowers on one plant and female flowers on another, so it is dioecious.
items.note: Same, one and different plants give monoecious, dioecious and the unisexual basic unit.

learn.title: Classifying flowers: symmetry, parts and sexes

blocks.text: Examiners build flower questions out of three independent axes of classification, and confusing them is the commonest source of lost marks. The first axis is symmetry. An actinomorphic flower can be cut into two equal halves by any plane passing through the centre, as a mustard or hibiscus flower can; the technical term is radial symmetry. A zygomorphic flower can be divided into two equal halves only by one particular plane, usually the vertical plane, as in a pea or bean flower with its typical butterfly shape; this is bilateral symmetry, and it matters ecologically because it forces an insect to enter the flower in one orientation, so pollen is placed on a predictable part of its body. The second axis is the presence or absence of parts: a complete flower carries all four whorls, an incomplete flower lacks at least one. The third axis is sex, where the presence of both androecium and gynoecium makes a flower bisexual and the presence of only one makes it unisexual.

blocks.caption: Flower classification on three axes
rows: Cut into equal halves by any plane through the centre
Cut into equal halves only by one vertical plane
Calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium all present
Both androecium and gynoecium in the same flower

items: Bisexual does not mean the flower self-pollinates; it only means both organs are present.
Complete and bisexual are independent: a flower can be complete but unisexual if it lacks one organ rather than one whorl, though most incomplete flowers are also unisexual.
In a zygomorphic flower the axis of symmetry is single and vertical, so the flower has an upper and a lower lip.
Pea flowers are zygomorphic and incomplete, which is why they are the standard example for both categories at once.
A flower's ovary position is described as superior when the other whorls arise below it and inferior when they arise above it.
A superior ovary is therefore hypogynous in insertion; an inferior ovary is perigynous or epigynous.
Apocarpous means the carpels are free, as in a buttercup; syncarpous means they are fused, as in a mustard or hibiscus.
A single flower borne alone on a stalk is a solitary inflorescence; a group of flowers on one axis is a cluster inflorescence.

items.text: Place a mustard flower on the table and pass a blade through the centre in any direction: every cut gives two matching halves, so it is actinomorphic. Try the same with a pea flower and only the cut along the keel works, so it is zygomorphic.
items.note: The physical test is the definition, and describing it earns the mark directly.

items.text: Hibiscus has five sepals, five petals, many stamens joined into a tube, and a five-branched style with five stigmas — a complete, bisexual, actinomorphic flower with a syncarpous gynoecium.
items.note: One flower lets you practise every axis of classification in a single answer.

blocks.text: The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is called inflorescence, and the two main patterns are defined by which bud opens first. In a racemose inflorescence the main axis grows indefinitely and the oldest flower is at the base, so new flowers are added at the tip — the growth is indefinite. The simplest form is a raceme, an unbranched elongated axis with stalked flowers, as in mustard and radix. If the pedicels are of unequal length so that all the flowers come to the same level, the inflorescence is a corymb, as in candytuft. If the stalks are so short that the flowers appear to sit directly on the base and they radiate from one point, it is an umbel, as in onion and cashew. If the flowers are stalkless and sit on an elongated axis it is a spike, as in plantain, and if the axis is flattened into a receptacle bearing sessile flowers it becomes a capitulum or head, as in sunflower and daisy. In a cymose inflorescence the main axis ends in a flower, so growth is definite and the oldest flower is at the top; the lateral buds then continue the cluster.

blocks.caption: Common inflorescence types
rows: Unbranched elongated axis with stalked flowers; oldest at base
Stalks of unequal length bringing flowers to one level
Flower stalks arise from one point like the ribs of an umbrella
Sessile flowers on an elongated unbranched axis
Sessile flowers on a flattened, cup-shaped receptacle
Main axis ends in a flower; oldest flower at top
A branched raceme, each branch itself a raceme
A spike of unisexual sessile flowers hanging down

items: Racemose means indefinite growth with the youngest flower at the apex; cymose means definite growth with the oldest flower at the apex.
A capitulum is called a head and is the hallmark of the sunflower family, where the ray florets look like petals but are individual flowers.
The umbel's flat, level platform gives a landing stage for insects, which is why umbels are common in insect-pollinated herbs.
Distinguishing a corymb from a raceme depends on the pedicels: unequal in a corymb so the top is level.
Inflorescence questions must state the arrangement and then give a plant example; one without the other is half an answer.
In a cyme the terminal flower opens first and the side branches take over, so the cluster keeps its definite plan.

items.text: A sunflower head shows a capitulum: the outer yellow ray florets and the inner disc florets are separate small flowers packed on a flat receptacle, so what looks like one flower is in fact a whole inflorescence.
items.note: This is the classic trap in identification — count the florets, not the colour.

items.text: In mustard the main axis keeps growing and bears flowers on stalks with the lowest one oldest, which identifies it as a raceme before you even count the parts.
items.note: Read growth and position first; they classify the inflorescence without needing floral counts.

blocks.text: Placentation is the arrangement of ovules within the ovary, and it follows directly from how many carpels the ovary is built from and how those carpels are joined. In marginal placentation a single carpel with one locus bears ovules along a ridge on the inner fused margin, the ventral suture, which is the pattern of the pea and the bean. In axile placentation the ovary is divided by septa into two or more loculi and the ovules hang from a central axis where the septa meet, as in the china rose, the tomato and the lemon. In parietal placentation the carpels are fused but no septa form, so the ovary has one locus and the ovules sit on the inner wall, often on outgrowths called placental columns; the mustard and the poppy follow this plan. Free central placentation arises when septa form and then break down, leaving the ovules on a central column that is not attached to the wall, as in the primrose and Dianthus. Basal placentation has a single ovule attached at the base of the ovary, as in the sunflower and the marigold, and this is the simplest of all.

blocks.caption: Types of placentation
rows: Ovules along the fused inner margin of one carpel
Ovules on a central axis where septa meet
Ovules on the inner wall of a single loculus
Ovules on a free-standing central column
A single ovule attached at the base of the ovary
Ovules on the inner surface of a septate ovary walls and septa

items: Marginal placentation is the signature of a single carpel, which is why the pea pod is the standard example.
Axile placentation requires septa, so a multilocular ovary with ovules at the centre is axile by definition.
Parietal placentation has fused carpels but no septa, giving one chamber with ovules scattered on the wall.
Free central placentation is best understood as axile placentation whose septa have been lost.
Basal placentation carries a single ovule, which means the resulting fruit holds one seed.
Placentation determines how many seeds a fruit can carry and how they are packed inside it.
The placenta is the tissue through which the developing seed is supplied with nutrients from the parent plant.
When asked to identify a type from a drawing, count the loculi first and then look for a central axis.

items.text: Cut a lemon across the middle and you see wedges separated by walls, each packed with juice sacs and seeds; the wedges are loculi and the seeds hang from the central axis, so the placentation is axile.
items.note: A kitchen example that can be cut open in a moment and still shows the whole arrangement.

items.text: Cut a pea pod along its stitched seam and the seeds are strung along that seam on a ridge, which is marginal placentation; the seam is the ventral suture of a single carpel.
items.note: The seam is the clue: one carpel, one row of seeds.

figures.caption: Figure: A bisexual flower in longitudinal section
figures.description: A flower cut vertically through the centre and opened out, showing the four whorls in order from the outside inwards. At the base sits the swollen receptacle carrying the pedicel below it. Four green sepals form the outer cup, four coloured petals within them, then several stamens each with a filament and a two-lobed anther, and at the centre a single carpel with a sticky stigma, a slender style and a swollen ovary containing two ovules.

figures.caption: Figure: Axile against parietal placentation
figures.description: Two circular cross-sections of ovaries. Left: the ovary is divided into four loculi by walls meeting at a central point, with ovules hung on that central axis, labelled axile, with a china rose as the example. Right: the ovary is a single chamber with no dividing walls and ovules attached in clusters to the inner wall, labelled parietal, with mustard as the example.

figures.caption: Figure: A raceme and a cyme compared
figures.description: Left panel: an unbranched axis that continues growing at its tip, with the largest, oldest flower at the bottom and progressively smaller younger flowers above it, marked indefinite growth. Right panel: the axis ends in a single large flower at the top, with side branches below bearing younger flowers, marked definite growth and oldest flower at the top.

keyPoints: A flower has four whorls on a receptacle: calyx of sepals, corolla of petals, androecium of stamens, gynoecium of carpels.
A stamen has a filament and a two-lobed anther; each anther lobe contains two pollen sacs in which pollen forms by meiosis.
A carpel has a stigma that catches pollen, a style, and an ovary containing ovules that become seeds after fertilisation.
Bisexual flowers have both androecium and gynoecium; unisexual flowers have only one, making them staminate or pistillate.
Complete flowers carry all four whorls; incomplete flowers lack at least one whorl.
Actinomorphic flowers have radial symmetry and can be halved by any plane through the centre; zygomorphic flowers have bilateral symmetry and one plane only.
Racemose inflorescence grows indefinitely with the youngest flower at the tip; cymose inflorescence grows definitely with the oldest flower at the tip.
Placentation is the arrangement of ovules in the ovary: marginal, axile, parietal, free central and basal.
The ovary matures into the fruit and each fertilised ovule matures into a seed.
Petals attract pollinators; sepals protect the flower while it is still in bud.
examFocus: A labelled diagram question wants each leader line straight, starting at the part and ending outside the flower, with the labels written horizontally on the right-hand side wherever possible.
Classification questions must name the axis being asked about — symmetry, completeness or sex — before giving the category, or the answer reads as guesswork.
Inflorescence answers need three things: the arrangement, whether growth is definite or indefinite, and one plant example.
Placentation is best identified from a cross-section: count the loculi, then decide whether ovules sit on a wall, a central axis, or the base.

vocabulary.meaning: The outer whorl of sepals protecting the bud.
The whorl of petals that attracts pollinators.
The female whorl of carpels, also called the pistil.
Radially symmetrical, halvable by any plane through the centre.
Bilaterally symmetrical, halvable only by one plane.
The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis.
The arrangement of ovules within the ovary.

questions.prompt: Which whorl of the flower protects the flower while it is still in bud and is usually green and leaf-like?
questions.explanation: The calyx is the outermost whorl, made of sepals, and its green leaf-like structure encloses the young bud and shields the delicate inner parts until the flower opens. The corolla is made of coloured petals for attracting insects, the androecium is the male stamens, and the gynoecium is the female carpels.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing calyx and corolla because both are protective or attractive whorls. C for calyx and cover is one way to keep them apart.

questions.prompt: The male part of a flower is the stamen, which consists of a stalk called the ______ and a terminal two-lobed ______ in which pollen grains are produced.
questions.explanation: The filament is the slender stalk that holds the anther up and positions it for pollen transfer, while the anther is the site of pollen formation: its two lobes each contain two pollen sacs in which pollen grains are produced by meiosis.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 'style' for the stalk. The style belongs to the carpel; the stamen's stalk is the filament.

questions.prompt: A flower has four sepals, four petals, six stamens and a gynoecium of two fused carpels, but only one plane divides it into two equal halves. How should it be described?
questions.explanation: All four whorls are present, so the flower is complete; both androecium and gynoecium are present, so it is bisexual; and only one plane of symmetry works, so it is zygomorphic. Each of the three terms answers a separate question — whorls present, organs present, and symmetry — which is why they must be assessed independently.
questions.commonMistake: Reading symmetry off the number of parts. Four petals does not make a flower radially symmetrical; the arrangement of those petals does.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between racemose and cymose inflorescence with one example of each.
questions.answer: In a racemose inflorescence the main axis grows indefinitely and does not end in a flower, so the oldest flower lies at the base and the youngest at the tip; mustard and radish show this pattern. In a cymose inflorescence the main axis ends in a flower, so its growth is definite, the oldest flower is at the top, and the younger flowers develop from lateral buds below it, as in jasmine and teak.
questions.explanation: The two distinguishing features are which end bears the oldest flower and whether the axis can keep growing. Both must be stated for each type, and an example follows. Comparing them as a pair, rather than describing one and assuming the other is understood, is what earns both marks.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the age positions. Racemose has the oldest at the bottom because the tip keeps producing new buds.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a bisexual flower under the four-whorled plan, naming the parts of each whorl and stating the function of each.
questions.answer: A bisexual flower arises on a swollen receptacle at the top of a stalk and bears four whorls. The outermost is the calyx, made of sepals, which protects the flower in bud and supports the open flower. Next is the corolla, made of coloured petals that often bear scent and nectar, whose function is to attract pollinating insects. The third is the androecium, the male whorl, consisting of stamens; each stamen has a filament supporting a two-lobed anther that produces pollen grains by meiosis. The innermost whorl is the gynoecium, made of carpels, each with a sticky stigma that receives pollen, a style down which the pollen tube grows, and an ovary containing ovules that develop into seeds after fertilisation. Because both androecium and gynoecium are present, the flower is bisexual.
questions.explanation: The answer must be built outside inwards, whorl by whorl, and each whorl needs both its parts and its function. Naming the parts with no function, or giving functions with no parts, leaves the question half answered, and the final sentence ties the description back to the term bisexual in the question.
questions.commonMistake: Describing only the visible petals and stamens. The calyx and the carpel's three parts are frequently omitted, and each omission costs a mark.

questions.prompt: In which of these would you expect to find marginal placentation?
questions.explanation: Marginal placentation occurs in a single carpel, where the ovules are strung along the fused inner margin or ventral suture, and both the pea and the bean pod show this arrangement. The china rose has axile placentation with a septate ovary, mustard has parietal placentation, and the sunflower has basal placentation with a single ovule.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing mustard because it appears in so many floral examples. Mustard is the standard example for parietal placentation, not marginal.

questions.prompt: A flower is described as having a small, dull green calyx, no coloured petals, numerous stamens but no carpels, and it grows in a drooping cluster on a tree. State whether it is complete, whether it is bisexual, and what kind of inflorescence is suggested, and explain the likely mode of pollination.
questions.answer: The flower is incomplete, because the corolla whorl is absent, so not all four whorls are present. It is unisexual, specifically staminate, because it bears stamens but no carpels. The drooping cluster suggests a catkin-type inflorescence of stalkless unisexual flowers hanging from the axis. The absence of coloured petals, the dull green colour and the pendulous cluster all indicate wind pollination: the flower has no need to attract insects, so it does not spend resources on a showy corolla, and the hanging arrangement lets the wind shake pollen free and carry it to a receptive stigma.
questions.explanation: Each observation must be read as evidence rather than merely recorded: no petals means incomplete, no carpels means staminate rather than bisexual, and a dull drooping cluster points to wind rather than insect pollination. The reasoning from appearance to mode of pollination is the part that carries the higher marks.
questions.commonMistake: Naming the categories without citing the feature that justified each one, which turns a four-mark question into two.

questions.prompt: State two functions of the corolla and one function of the calyx, and explain why wind-pollinated flowers have a reduced corolla.
questions.answer: The corolla attracts pollinating insects through its brightly coloured petals and often bears scent or nectar as a reward, and it also protects the inner stamens and carpels while the flower is in bud. The calyx protects the developing flower in the bud stage and supports the open flower. Wind-pollinated flowers reduce the corolla because colour, scent and nectar exist to lure animals; an unseen wind needs no lure, so resources are diverted into producing large quantities of lightweight pollen instead.
questions.explanation: Two corolla functions and one calyx function are asked for, and the final explanation links structure to the mode of pollination: the corolla is costly and pointless where the pollinator is the wind, which is exactly why grasses and maize have small, inconspicuous flowers.
questions.commonMistake: Saying wind-pollinated flowers have no corolla at all. They usually retain a small, reduced one; the point is reduction, not absence.

questions.prompt: Placentation is the arrangement of __________ within the ovary. When the ovary is divided by septa into two or more loculi and the ovules are attached to a central axis, the type is __________ placentation.
questions.explanation: Placentation refers specifically to how ovules are arranged and attached inside the ovary, which is what determines how seeds are packed in the fruit. Axile placentation requires both a septate ovary with several loculi and ovules hung on the central column where the septa meet, as in the china rose, tomato and lemon.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 'seeds' for the first blank. The ovules are what are attached; seeds exist only after fertilisation.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a cymose inflorescence is correct?
options: The main axis grows indefinitely and the youngest flower is at the tip
The oldest flower is at the base and new flowers are added above it
The main axis ends in a flower, so growth is definite and the oldest flower is at the top
The flowers have stalks of unequal length so that they all reach one level
questions.answer: The main axis ends in a flower, so growth is definite and the oldest flower is at the top
questions.explanation: Cymose inflorescence is defined by definite growth: the terminal bud becomes a flower and can grow no further, so subsequent flowers arise from lateral branches below it and the oldest flower sits at the apex. The other options describe racemose growth or the corymb, which is a racemose type with unequal pedicels.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the option mentioning unequal pedicels because it sounds technical; that describes a corymb, which is racemose.

questions.prompt: A student counts the parts of a flower and finds five sepals, five petals, a ring of stamens, and an ovary divided into three loculi with ovules on a central axis where the walls meet. Identify the placentation type, state whether the ovary is unilocular or multilocular, and name a plant with the same arrangement.
questions.answer: The placentation is axile, because the ovary is divided by septa into several loculi — here three — and the ovules are attached to the central axis where those septa meet. The ovary is multilocular, having three chambers rather than one. A plant with the same arrangement is the china rose, the tomato, the lemon or the onion, all of which show axile placentation with ovules hung from a central column.
questions.explanation: Identification comes from two features working together: the presence of septa dividing the ovary into loculi rules out parietal and free central, and the central axis of attachment rules in axile. Counting loculi gives the multilocular answer, and the example must be one that genuinely shows axile placentation.
questions.commonMistake: Naming parietal placentation because ovules appear to be near the wall. Parietal placentation has no septa at all, so the presence of dividing walls excludes it immediately.
